Notes

Overview

Cleft lip ± cleft palate is a common congenital craniofacial deformity. It occurs in three forms:

Cleft lip alone Always the upper lip. Mainly cosmetic / psychosocial, with mild feeding difficulty.·Cleft palate alone Oral–nasal communication → feeding, speech, ear and dental problems.·Combined cleft lip + palate Both defects; each is repaired at its own age window.
For every case, cover these five principles
Risk factors·Anatomic defect·Health effects·Treatment·Timing of surgery
Notes

Etiology & Risk Factors

<1%

2–4%

~7%

Other risk factors

Advanced parental age
Associated syndromes / craniofacial abnormalities, including Down syndrome
Maternal smoking during pregnancy
1st-trimester maternal medications, especially antineoplastics and anticonvulsants

Nutritional factors (folate, protein) were mentioned in lecture but not emphasized as major causes.

Exam move
Be ready to name 1–2 risk factors: lead with family history, then add one such as maternal smoking or 1st-trimester anticonvulsants.

Cleft Lip

  • Unilateral / bilateral
  • Complete / Incomplete

Defect

  • Skin
  • Mucosa
  • Orbicularis oris
  • Nasal cartilage
Notes

Cleft Lip

Classification

★ Exam

Answering an image question

★ Exam

Give the full diagnosis: side + extent + "cleft lip".

Left unilateral incomplete cleft lip·Left unilateral complete cleft lip·Bilateral incomplete cleft lip·Bilateral complete cleft lip
What the image showsWhat you describe
Closed mouthThe lip only
Open mouth with the palate visibleLip + palate
Palate onlyThe palate only
Don't overcall
Do not comment on the palate unless the mouth/palate is actually shown. Bilateral clefts may be symmetrical or asymmetrical; exam images usually show an obvious complete/incomplete pattern.

Epidemiology: which pattern is commoner

Unilateral > bilateral·Left > right·Incomplete > complete

No clear explanation for the left-sided predominance was given.

Anatomic defect

★ Exam
Skin — deficient / discontinuous

Associated nasal deformity

Nostril shape becomes abnormal.
Orbicularis oris muscle — key muscle
Nasal cartilage is present but hypoplastic / displaced.
Adjacent nasal / facial skeletal structures may also be affected.
Oral mucosa — deficient / discontinuous
Key muscle
Cleft lip → orbicularis oris.

Clinical effects of an isolated cleft lip (no cleft palate)

DomainEffect
Cosmetic / psychosocialMain problem
FeedingMild difficulty: infant cannot form an adequate seal around the breast/nipple. Usually managed with appropriate nipples.
SpeechNot significantly affected
HearingNot significantly affected
Initial management
Educate the family about feeding
Special feeding nipples
Feed upright
Small, frequent feeds to reduce the infant's effort

Clinical Impact

  • Feeding (difficult to make a proper seal)
  • Psychosocial

Management

  • Educations (proper feeding: special nipple, feeding upright, frequent feeds)
  • Surgery – cleft lip repair
  • At the age of 3-6 months
  • Rule of 10s:
    • Weight 10 lbs
    • Hb 10
    • 10 weeks
  • Baby with a cleft palate, feeding problems and poor weight gain (5 kg) — to prepare for surgery → insert a nasogastric tube (secure nutrition). 436
Notes

Cleft Lip Repair

Timing: 3–6 months

★ Exam
Why not before ~3 monthsThe usual window: 3–6 monthsWhy not after ~6 months
Avoid unnecessary very early surgery; let the infant grow, confirm adequate general health and identify other problems.Infant is big and healthy enough, but not yet mobile or on solids.Child becomes more mobile and progresses toward solid feeding → post- op care is harder.
Delayed repair can still achieve a similar result; 3–6 months is the usual timing, not an absolute deadline.

Rule of 10s

★★★ Top yield

Before cleft-lip repair, the infant should meet all three:

10 weeks Age ≥ 10 weeks·10 lb Weight ≥ 10 lb (≈ 4.5 kg)·10 g/dL Hemoglobin ≥ 10 g/dL

Weight and Hb act as indicators of the infant's overall health and nutrition.

Failing the Rule of 10s
Think malnutrition (often from inadequate feeding technique) or an underlying medical problem. Routine extensive screening for congenital abnormalities is not needed in an otherwise well infant.

Surgical principle

Reconstruct the lip in layers: mucosa, orbicularis oris muscle, skin. Goal: restore lip continuity and improve symmetry, including partial correction of the nasal deformity.

The nose and rhinoplasty

Staged approach
Nasal shape is improved during early cleft surgery, but definitive / full rhinoplasty is postponed. Many patients need a later definitive rhinoplasty.
Why not do it all early
Aggressive rhinoplasty in a young child can cause scarring and interfere with facial / nasal growth.

Cleft Palate

  • Bifid uvula
  • Soft palate only
  • Soft and hard palate
  • Combined cleft lip an palate
Added explanationEmbryology: the lip and primary palate (the premaxilla in front of the incisive foramen) form at about 4–7 weeks; the secondary palate (hard and soft palate behind it) fuses at about 8–12 weeks.
  • Gestational age when the primary palate develops → 4–8 weeks. 434 ×2
Notes

Cleft Palate

Pattern: posterior → anterior

Unlike cleft lip (which extends from the lip toward the nose), a cleft palate progresses from back to front:

Uvula·Soft palate·Hard palate·Alveolar / anterior region

Posterior (back)

There is no useful unilateral/bilateral classification for the palate, unlike cleft lip.

Anterior (front)

Types, from mildest to most extensive

Bifid / cleft uvula

Soft-palate cleft

Soft + hard palate cleft

Complete cleft lip and palate

RegionPositionBone
Soft palatePosteriorNo underlying bone
Hard palateAnteriorBony

Normal function and the anatomic defect

Function of the palate
Main function: separate the oral cavity from the nasal cavity. A cleft creates an oral–nasal communication.
LayerNormal palateCleft palate
Oral + nasal mucosaContinuous layers separating the two cavitiesSeparated → oral–nasal communication
Palatal musclesContinuous, normally attachedDiscontinuous / abnormally attached
Bone (anterior)Present under the hard palateAnterior clefts may have bony deficiency
Surgical implication
The palatal muscle must be repaired, not just the mucosal opening closed.
Source key vs the lecture: a bilateral complete cleft with a very short columella and small prolabium at 4 months was keyed "bony alveolus" as the hardest part. The alveolar bone gap is not repaired at 4 months — it is bone-grafted when the canines erupt (the same exam's next question). The stem's clue is the nose: in bilateral clefts the short columella makes nasal correction the most difficult part. Answer here: nasal position.
  • 4-month-old, bilateral complete cleft, very short columella, small prolabium — most difficult part of the repair → nasal position (columella/nose). 436

Defect

  • Oral mucosa
  • Nasal mucosa
  • Tensor veli palatini muscle
  • Bone (maxilla)

Clinical Impact

  • Feeding (unable to make a proper seal, weak swallowing, nasal regurgitation)
  • Speech abnormalities
  • Repeated ear infections
  • Dental
  • Facial growth
Notes

Clinical Effects of Cleft Palate

★ Exam

Cleft palate has more functional and medical consequences than an isolated cleft lip.

DomainMechanismResultManagement / follow-up
FeedingCannot form a proper seal; ineffective swallowing / suctionNasal regurgitation, poor feedingSpecial nipples, upright feeding, frequent smaller feeds
SpeechPalate generates normal oral pressure; cleft lets air escape into the noseSpeech abnormalitiesSpeech therapy
Ear / hearingPalatal dysfunction disturbs middle-ear pressure regulationRecurrent middle-ear problems / infectionsENT follow-up
DentalAbnormal palate / alveolar structuresDental problemsDentistry follow-up
Multidisciplinary team
Plastic / cleft surgery·Speech therapy·ENT·Dentistry

Management

  • Educations (proper feeding: special nipple, feeding upright, frequent feeds)
  • Surgery – Cleft palate repair
  • At the age of 12-18 months
Notes

Cleft Palate Repair

Timing: 12–18 months

★★★ Top yield

Main aim: repair before significant speech development, i.e. before ~2 years.

Why not laterWhy not much earlier
The child should learn speech with the palate already closed. After speech patterns develop, the child may form abnormal compensatory habits and avoid sounds needing oral pressure. These learned patterns persist and need retraining even after anatomical repair.Surgery is deep inside a small oral cavity; the palate and mouth must be big enough for adequate exposure and instruments. Some children can technically be repaired at ~10 months, but 12– 18 months is the usual preferred range.
Surgical principle
1 Raise tissue flaps from both sides·2 Mobilize them medially·3 Reconstruct the palatal musculature·4 Close the central defect in layers

Goal: eliminate the oral–nasal communication.

Speech after repair
Surgery improves speech but may not normalize it completely. The palatal muscles were developmentally abnormal / displaced and, even reconstructed, are not equivalent to normal anatomy, so continued speech therapy may be needed.
  • Most important factor in deciding cleft palate surgery → dental and mouth examination (the mouth/palate must be big enough; age 12–18 months is the guide). 436
Notes

Timing at a Glance

Birth≥10 wkCleft lip repair Lip 3–6 mo once the Rule of 10s is met; later repair still possible 3 moCleft palate repair before speech patterns develop 6 mo 9 moPalate 12–18 mo ~10 mo 12 mo 15 mo18 mo~2 years major speech development 21 mo24 mo
  • 5-year-old after palate repair with nasal speech not responding to exercises → velopharyngeal insufficiency. 436
  • Timing of bone grafting in cleft palate → when the canine teeth come out. 436

Exam Focus: Lip vs Palate Side by Side

For any cleft case or image, work down these rows.

★★★ Top yield
Cleft lip
DiagnosisSide + extent, e.g. left unilateral complete; extends lip → nose
Cleft palate

By extent: uvula → soft → hard → alveolar (posterior → anterior); no uni/bilateral

Risk factors
Family history (most important), parental age, maternal smoking, syndromes (Down), 1st-trimester antineoplastics / anticonvulsants

Tissues

Skin, muscle, oral mucosa + nasal deformity

Oral + nasal mucosa, muscle, ± bone anteriorly

Key muscle
Orbicularis oris
Palatal musculature

Feeding

Mild (poor seal)

Significant: poor seal, ineffective suction, nasal regurgitation

Speech
Not significantly affected
Abnormal (air escapes nasally) → speech therapy

Ear / hearing

Not significantly affected

Recurrent middle-ear disease → ENT

Other
Main issue cosmetic / psychosocial
Dental problems → dentistry

Early management

Feeding education, special nipples, upright feeding, small frequent feeds

Repair timing
3–6 months, after the Rule of 10s
12–18 months, before ~2 years / speech

Operation

Layered: mucosa, orbicularis oris, skin; partial nasal correction

Bilateral flaps, medial mobilization, muscle reconstruction, layered closure

Long term
Later definitive rhinoplasty often needed
Continued speech therapy may be needed
Added explanationVelopharyngeal insufficiency (VPI) — after palate repair the soft palate may still fail to close off the nasopharynx during speech → hypernasal speech and nasal air escape not fixed by exercises → speech assessment (nasendoscopy) and a secondary operation (pharyngoplasty or pharyngeal flap). Alveolar bone grafting of the alveolar cleft is done in mixed dentition, before the permanent canine erupts (~8–11 years), so the canine can come through grafted bone.
Notes

Mastery Checklist

1 Family history is the most important identifiable risk factor: <1% → 2–4% (one first-degree relative) → ~7% (two).
2 Cleft lip is always upper lip; classify by side (unilateral L/R vs bilateral) + extent (incomplete = doesn't reach the nose;
complete = reaches it). Commoner: unilateral, left, incomplete.
3 On an image, describe only what is shown; no palate comment on a closed-mouth photo.
4 Cleft lip layers: skin, orbicularis oris, oral mucosa; nasal cartilage is present but hypoplastic / displaced.
5 Isolated cleft lip = cosmetic / psychosocial + mild feeding trouble; speech and hearing are spared.
6 Lip repair at 3–6 months once the Rule of 10s is met: ≥10 weeks, ≥10 lb (≈4.5 kg), Hb ≥10 g/dL. Failing it → malnutrition
or an underlying problem.
7 Definitive rhinoplasty is delayed: aggressive early surgery scars and impairs nasal/facial growth.
8 Cleft palate runs posterior → anterior (uvula → soft → hard → alveolar); repair must reconstruct the palatal muscle, not
just close mucosa.
9 Palate effects: feeding (nasal regurgitation), speech, recurrent middle-ear disease, dental → multidisciplinary team.
10 Palate repair at 12–18 months, before speech develops (~2 years); speech may still need therapy afterward.
  • Most common site → left. 436
